doc.title: Lanny Morgan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

chapter: Early road bands and the Army
title: Big bands and road work in the 1950s
summary: Studios hired no doublers, so road bands were the path; big bands faded late in the 1950s but Maynard's still drew crowds.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: So at least you decided well I am going to still pursue this. It didn’t knock you out of the thought of doing it.

No because I did meet people and there were plans — you know you’d meet somebody and I’m sure you know how that is too. People say hey you know, so-and-so’s going out in two weeks. And it was mostly all road work at that time because the studios at that time weren’t really employing doublers, not many doublers if any. They were all straight flute players, straight oboe players, straight this player and so forth. And they were all on staff, Paramount and MGM and Twentieth Century. So there was not even any thought of that. So it was all, you know there were maybe 40, 45 bands in this country that you could think about going with. The Dorseys and Benny Goodman and —
Yeah. I guess I had this fairly misconstrued idea that the big bands almost like disappeared in the latter 40s. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

No I think they – they weren’t as hot as they were. But I think the big bands didn’t — well I think they were really almost over at the end of the 50s. Because both Dorseys were alive then. Benny was still alive then. Even the bands like Henry Busse and bands that people really didn’t want to go out with but they would to get road experience. But when I was on Maynard’s band in the 60s, the first half of the 60s, we used to play dances and there was standing room only. And there were a lot of kids too, which was amazing. I wish it was that way today.
